Sortable

<loomi-sortable> — a SortableJS-inspired drag-and-drop list. Provide rows via the items array ({ id, label, meta?, locked?, filtered?, className? }) and read the new order back from the reorder event. Give two or more lists the same group to let users drag items between them — a Kanban board’s columns, for example.

Basic Usage

Section titled “Basic Usage”

A Secondary Line per Row

Section titled “A Secondary Line per Row”

meta renders as a smaller line beneath label — useful for a due date, a subtitle, or an assignee.

Reacting to a Reorder

Section titled “Reacting to a Reorder”

The reorder event fires after dragging a row within the same list, with the full new order of ids.

Shared Lists

Section titled “Shared Lists”

Give two or more <loomi-sortable> elements the same non-empty group and users can drag a row from one straight into another — exactly what a “To Do / In Progress / Done” board needs. Lists with no group (or a different one) stay independent.

To Do

In Progress

Done

When an item moves across lists, transfer fires on both lists involved — once on the list that lost it, once on the one that gained it — each with that list’s own resulting order. Listen on whichever lists you care about to persist the new column.

An empty list still accepts a drop — it shows a “Drop here” hint so the target is visible even with zero rows.

Cloning

Section titled “Cloning”

Use clone or group.pull = "clone" to copy items into another list while leaving the source list unchanged.

Palette

Canvas

Disabling Sorting

Section titled “Disabling Sorting”

Set sort = false to prevent reordering within a list while still allowing items to be dragged into another compatible list. Set sortable = false only when the list should not start drags at all.

Templates

Plan

Handles

Section titled “Handles”

Set has-handle or the SortableJS-style handle property to make rows draggable only from the built-in grip.

Filter

Section titled “Filter”

Set filter to a selector and mark rows with className or filtered. Filtered and locked rows do not start drags and emit a filter event when clicked or drag-started.

MultiDrag

Section titled “MultiDrag”

Set multi-drag or the multiDrag property to let users click-select rows and drag the selected set together.

Swap

Section titled “Swap”

Set swap to swap the dragged row with the hovered row instead of shifting rows in between.

Reacting to a Click (Not a Drag)

Section titled “Reacting to a Click (Not a Drag)”

item-click fires when a row is clicked without being dragged — native drag-and-drop suppresses the browser’s own click event after an actual drag, so this only fires for genuine clicks. Useful for opening a detail view.

Saving the Order

Section titled “Saving the Order”

Persist the new order from reorder (or transfer) — e.g. via a fetch call to your backend.

Read the current order at any time via the order property, without waiting for an event.

Attributes

Section titled “Attributes”
AttributeDefaultDescription
items[]Rows to display/reorder — { id, label, meta? }[] (property or JSON).
group(blank)String group name, or JS property object { name, pull, put }.
clonefalseClone dragged items into another shared list instead of moving them.
sorttrueEnable same-list sorting. When false, compatible outbound drags still work.
sortabletrueEnable drag-starting from the list.
has-handlefalseDrag rows only from the built-in handle.
handle(blank)SortableJS-style handle selector; enables the built-in handle.
filter(blank)Selector for rows/elements that should not drag.
multi-dragfalseClick-select multiple rows and drag them together.
swapfalseSwap the dragged row with the hovered row.

Property: order (array of ids). Events: reorder (detail: { order }, same-list drag), transfer (detail: { order, items }, fired on both lists after a cross-list move), filter (detail: { item }), item-click (detail: { item }, a click outside multi-drag mode).

Full Example

Section titled “Full Example”

Framework integration

Section titled “Framework integration”

<loomi-sortable> is a standard custom element, so the browser can use it in plain HTML, Blade, React, Vue, Angular, Svelte, Astro, and most other frameworks. The important beginner rule is: install the package, import it once before the tag is rendered, then write the Loomi tag in your template.

Where to run commands

Section titled “Where to run commands”

Run install commands from the app where you want to use this component. That means the folder that contains that app’s package.json. Do not run these install commands from packages/sortable unless you are editing LoomiUI itself.

If you are contributing to LoomiUI itself, first move to the top-level components folder. That is where the main package.json for all packages lives, and pnpm --filter ... commands should be run from there:

Plain HTML

Section titled “Plain HTML”

Use the CDN version for prototypes, documentation pages, or a quick reproduction. The import map tells the browser where to find Lit, which Loomi components use internally.

Bundlers and single-page apps

Section titled “Bundlers and single-page apps”

In Vite, Webpack, Parcel, Rollup, or a framework build pipeline, install the package and import it once in your main app JavaScript file. After that, you can use the Loomi tag anywhere in your app.

This component accepts items as a JavaScript property. Use an HTML attribute only for simple strings; use a property when you pass arrays, objects, or functions.

Laravel Blade

Section titled “Laravel Blade”

Run the install command from your Laravel project root, then import the component in resources/js/app.js. If your project uses Laravel Vite, npm run dev and npm run build should also be run from the Laravel project root.

React

Section titled “React”

React can render Loomi tags directly. If you are on React 18, or if you need to pass arrays, objects, or functions, use a ref and assign those values after the component mounts.

If TypeScript does not recognize the Loomi tag in JSX, add it to your app’s JSX type declarations.

Vue

Section titled “Vue”

Import the package in the component that uses it, or once in your main Vue file. Vue templates can use Loomi tags directly. For arrays, objects, or functions, pass the value as a JavaScript property instead of as plain text.

If Vue warns that the tag is an unknown component, configure compilerOptions.isCustomElement for tags that start with loomi- in your Vite or Vue config.

Angular

Section titled “Angular”

Import the package once and tell Angular to allow custom HTML tags with CUSTOM_ELEMENTS_SCHEMA. For NgModule apps, add the schema to the module instead of the standalone component.

Svelte and Astro

Section titled “Svelte and Astro”

Svelte can import the package inside a component script. Astro can import it in the frontmatter of the page or layout where the tag appears.

Server-side rendering notes

Section titled “Server-side rendering notes”

Frameworks such as Next.js, Nuxt, SvelteKit, and Astro sometimes render HTML on the server before browser-only code runs. If your framework complains, move the Loomi import to client-side code. In Next.js, that usually means a component with "use client"; in Nuxt, it often means a .client.ts plugin.
